### 51. Protected raw-array `assign()` can read from freed self-owned storage when the input buffer aliases the receiver

Protected/documented route: `unlimited_int::assign(const uint32_t*, size_t)` and `unlimited_int::assign(const uint64_t*, size_t)` are declared as protected helpers in `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:108-111`; the adjacent comments say they are used by the raw-array constructors but "can also be used independently". A derived class can expose those helpers and can also access the protected `intarrays` backing storage.

Root: both raw-array overloads destroy or flush the receiver before they validate/copy any non-empty source buffer. The `uint32_t` overload calls `this->flush()` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/assign.cpp:8-9`, then only after that calls `increase_until_num_of_ints()` and starts reading `arr[counter_ints]` at `assign.cpp:19-32`. The `uint64_t` overload has the same ordering at `assign.cpp:60-71` and reads `arr[counter_ints]` at `assign.cpp:95`. `flush()` sends the old arrays to the thread-local piggy bank at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.cpp:14-23`. If the flushed receiver is larger than `PIGGY_BANK_MAXIMUM`, `int_array_piggy_bank::obey_PIGGY_BANK_MAXIMUM()` destroys cached arrays at `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array_piggy_bank.cpp:71-78`, and `int_array::destroy()` performs the actual `delete[]` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array.cpp:222-228`. Therefore a valid source pointer into the receiver's own backing storage at call entry can be freed before `assign()` performs its first source read.

Observed effect: a derived test class constructed an `unlimited_int` with `PIGGY_BANK_MAXIMUM + 4` `uint32_t` limbs, took a pointer to the first protected backing array, and then called the documented protected `assign(const uint32_t*, size_t)` helper with that pointer and the first node's length. Both debug and release-style ASan/UBSan builds reported a heap-use-after-free at `unlimited/unlimited_int/assign.cpp:32`. A sibling `uint64_t` probe constructed through the protected `uint64_t` raw-array constructor and called `assign(const uint64_t*, size_t)` with a pointer into the first backing node; release-style ASan/UBSan reported the same heap-use-after-free at `unlimited/unlimited_int/assign.cpp:95`.

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_raw_self_alias_uaf_probe.cpp` for `uint32_t` and `/tmp/unlimited_int_raw64_self_alias_uaf_probe.cpp` for `uint64_t`. The `uint32_t` route reproduced with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1` and with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`; the `uint64_t` route reproduced with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`. All runs used ASan/UBSan and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=4` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=4`. The release-style `uint32_t` repro reports:

```text
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free
READ of size 4
#0 unlimited::unlimited_int::assign(unsigned int const*, unsigned long) unlimited/unlimited_int/assign.cpp:32
freed by:
#1 unlimited::int_array::destroy() unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array.cpp:227
#2 unlimited::int_array_piggy_bank::obey_PIGGY_BANK_MAXIMUM() unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array_piggy_bank.cpp:77
#5 unlimited::unlimited_int::flush() unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.cpp:19
```

Distinctness: this is not finding #27. Finding #27 is a late-cleanup false `bad_alloc` after raw-array assignment has committed a leading-zero-stripped value. This finding is a no-OOM read-after-free before the raw-array copy completes, caused by accepting a source buffer that is valid at call entry but aliases storage invalidated by the receiver's own pre-copy `flush()`. It also differs from the protected raw-array null-pointer candidate rejected earlier in the ledger: the source pointer here is non-null and valid when the call starts.

### 52. Protected `copy_most_significant_to()` can flip the old destination sign before throwing `bad_alloc`

Protected/documented route: `unlimited_int::copy_most_significant_to(unlimited_int&, size_t) const` is declared as a protected helper in `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:128-130`. Its comments say the destination "doesn't need to be prepared", that the helper copies the most-significant portion of the source into the least-significant portion of the destination, and that it causes the destination to be non-negative.

Root: the helper clears the destination sign before it performs the growth allocation needed for the copy. `unlimited/unlimited_int/copy.cpp:120` assigns `num_to_paste_into._is_negative = false`, then `copy.cpp:129` calls `num_to_paste_into.increase_until_num_of_ints(num_of_ints_to_copy_cpy)`. If the destination needs more storage and that allocation throws, the requested copy has not completed, but the destination's previous sign has already been committed. A caller that catches `std::bad_alloc` observes a mutated old destination value instead of either the old value or a completed copy.

Observed effect: a derived probe exposed `copy_most_significant_to()`, created a large positive source, initialized the destination to `-12345`, and forced the first allocation inside `source.copy_most_to(destination, 6U)` to throw. After catching `std::bad_alloc`, the destination printed as `12345`. Both debug and release-style builds reproduced:

```text
before=-12345
after=12345
copy_most_badalloc_sign_mutation=reproduced
```

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_copy_most_badalloc_probe.cpp`, `/tmp/unlimited_int_copy_most_badalloc_probe_dbg`, and `/tmp/unlimited_int_copy_most_badalloc_probe_rel`. The debug build used `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`; the release-style build used `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`. Both used `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=1` so the destination growth path was deterministic.

Distinctness: this is not the non-owning-view `copy_most_significant_to()` corruption from #42, because the destination here is an ordinary owning `unlimited_int`. It is not full copy-assignment false-throw finding #25, and it is not raw-array assignment findings #27/#51. This is a separate protected-helper exception-safety failure: a failed partial-copy helper can silently change the sign of an unrelated pre-existing destination value before the allocation that was required to perform the copy.

### 53. Protected `split_at()` clears both output signs before growth allocations, so `bad_alloc` can mutate unrelated old outputs

Protected/documented route: `unlimited_int::split_at(size_t, unlimited_int*, unlimited_int*) const` is declared as a protected helper in `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:197-198`, with the comment that it splits the receiver into significant and insignificant parts based on the number of limbs to put in `low`.

Root: after validating only that `high` and `low` are distinct pointers, the non-trivial split path clears both output signs before it prepares either output's storage. `unlimited/unlimited_int/split_at.cpp:31-32` assigns `high->_is_negative = false` and `low->_is_negative = false`, then `split_at.cpp:35-36` calls `low->increase_until_num_of_ints(length_of_low)` and `high->increase_until_num_of_ints(length_of_high)`. If either output needs more storage and allocation fails, the split has not completed, but the old output values have already been sign-mutated.

Observed effect: a derived probe exposed `split_at()`, used an ordinary large positive source, initialized `high` to `-22222` and `low` to `-11111`, then forced the first allocation inside `source.split_to(3U, high, low)` to throw. After catching `std::bad_alloc`, both unrelated destination objects had changed sign:

```text
high_before=-22222
high_after=22222
low_before=-11111
low_after=11111
split_at_badalloc_sign_mutation=reproduced
```

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_at_badalloc_probe.cpp`, `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_at_badalloc_probe_dbg`, and `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_at_badalloc_probe_rel`. The debug build used `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`; the release-style build used `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`. Both used `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=1`.

Distinctness: this is not #52, although the exception-safety class is similar. Finding #52 is a single-destination `copy_most_significant_to()` partial-copy helper. This finding is the two-output `split_at()` helper, and a failed split can mutate both pre-existing outputs before either half of the requested split is committed. It also differs from the non-owning-view and destructive Karatsuba findings because the probe uses ordinary owning `unlimited_int` outputs and does not alias the source.

### 54. Protected `multiply_karatsuba_destroy_this_and_num_to_mult()` returns zero for large self-aliasing operands

Protected route: `unlimited_int::multiply_karatsuba_destroy_this_and_num_to_mult(unlimited_int*)` is declared as a protected helper in `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:194`. The declaration and implementation reject only `nullptr`; they do not state or enforce that `num_to_mult` must be distinct from `this`. The basecase branch also behaves as if self-aliasing is supported: it computes the answer first with `multiply_basecase(num_to_mult, &answer)` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/multiplication_Karatsuba.cpp:97-103`, then flushes both aliases only after the answer exists.

Root: in the recursive Karatsuba branch, the helper destructively splits `this` before it splits `num_to_mult`. `unlimited/unlimited_int/multiplication_Karatsuba.cpp:110-112` creates `high1/low1/high2/low2`, calls `this->split_at_and_use_original(m2, &high1, &low1)`, and then calls `num_to_mult->split_at_and_use_original(m2, &high2, &low2)`. If `num_to_mult == this`, the first call consumes and flushes the only operand; `split_at_and_use_original()` explicitly routes through a temporary when an output aliases `this` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/split_at.cpp:222-237`, and its all-distinct path detaches source nodes and resets the source counters at `split_at.cpp:239-266`. The second split therefore runs on the already-consumed zero receiver, so `high2` and `low2` become zero and the recursive multiplication collapses to zero.

Observed effect: a derived probe exposed the protected helper and called `x.multiply_karatsuba_destroy_this_and_num_to_mult(&x)` on a 96-limb non-power-of-two positive value. The control result was the public `x * x`, which produced a large nonzero square. The protected self-aliasing call returned `0` in both debug and release-style sanitizer builds:

```text
0
karatsuba_self_alias=mismatch
```

The same probe with a 10-limb value stayed on the basecase branch and printed `karatsuba_self_alias=ok` in both builds, confirming that the failure is the recursive destructive split ordering rather than self-aliasing in `multiply_basecase()`.

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_karatsuba_self_alias_probe.cpp`, `/tmp/unlimited_int_karatsuba_self_alias_probe_dbg`, and `/tmp/unlimited_int_karatsuba_self_alias_probe_rel`. The debug build used `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`; the release-style build used `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`. Both used ASan/UBSan and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=2`.

Distinctness: this is not the public `operator*=` bad-allocation mutation from #28 and not the non-owning-view ownership failures from #49/#50. The probe uses an ordinary owning object and no allocation failure. It is also narrower than public self multiplication, which still goes through `power2()` / `power2_destroy_this()` or `multiply_karatsuba_destroy_this(const unlimited_int*)` and was covered by prior public oracles. This finding is the protected two-destroy Karatsuba helper's missing self-alias precondition/handling at the recursive threshold.

### 55. Protected `split_at_and_use_original()` can erase old output values before throwing `bad_alloc`

Protected route: `unlimited_int::split_at_and_use_original(const size_t, unlimited_int*, unlimited_int*)` is declared as a protected helper at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:201`. Its comments state that `low` or `high` can alias `this`, but that `high` and `low` must be distinct. The all-distinct non-trivial path is reachable by derived classes and by internal arithmetic helpers.

Root: in the all-distinct path, the helper destroys both output objects before allocating their replacement backing lists. `unlimited/unlimited_int/split_at.cpp:239-244` calls `high->flush()`, then `low->flush()`, then allocates `low->intarrays = new list_of_int_arrays` and `high->intarrays = new list_of_int_arrays`. `flush()` in `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.cpp:14-24` sets `auto_destroy = true`, frees/deposits the old list if present, nulls `intarrays`, and calls `set_to_zero()`. If the first replacement-list allocation throws, both outputs have already lost their old values even though the split did not complete.

Observed effect: a derived probe exposed the protected helper, initialized `high = -22222` and `low = -11111`, then armed a global allocation failer only around `source.split_at_and_use_original(3, &high, &low)`. On the first allocation after arming, the call threw `std::bad_alloc`; afterward both old outputs had been erased:

```text
split_original_badalloc_output_mutation fail_index=0 allocations_seen=1
high_before=-22222
high_after=0
low_before=-11111
low_after=0
```

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_original_badalloc_probe.cpp`, `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_original_badalloc_probe_dbg`, and `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_original_badalloc_probe_rel`. The debug build used `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`; the release-style build used `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`. Both used `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=1` and a scoped global allocation failer.

Distinctness: this is not #53. Finding #53 is the plain const `split_at()` helper clearing the signs of existing output objects before allocation, leaving old magnitudes with positive signs after a throw. This finding is the destructive `split_at_and_use_original()` helper erasing the old output magnitudes completely through `flush()` before allocation. It is also not #28's public `operator*=` destructive-source mutation and not the non-owning-view ownership failures; the probe uses ordinary owning objects and fails before any source-node detachment.

### 56. Public null C-string assignment bypasses the library's guarded parser and constructs `std::string(nullptr)`

Public route: `unlimited_int x; x = nullptr;`

Root: the public API has a guarded C-string construction/parsing path: `unlimited_int(const char*, unsigned)` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:309` calls `unlimited_int::from_string(const char*, unsigned)`, and that overload rejects null at `unlimited/unlimited_int/from_string.cpp:88-89`. Assignment does not have the same C-string overload. The only public string assignment is `void operator=(const std::string& str_num)` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:316`. Therefore `x = nullptr` is accepted by overload resolution by first constructing a temporary `std::string` from the null pointer, before any `unlimited_int` null check can run.

Observed effect: `unlimited_int x(123); x = nullptr;` throws from the standard library on this libstdc++ build: `std::logic_error: basic_string: construction from null is not valid`, while `unlimited_int y(nullptr);` throws the library's intended `std::invalid_argument: Can't convert null string to unlimited_int`. On a standard-library implementation that does not diagnose the null precondition, the public assignment route reaches undefined behavior before entering the library's parser. The receiver remained `123` in the observed run only because libstdc++ threw before the assignment body executed.

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_null_assign_probe.cpp` built and run under ASan/UBSan. Output: `assign St11logic_error:basic_string: construction from null is not valid after=123` and `ctor St16invalid_argument:Can't convert null string to unlimited_int`.

Distinctness: this is not findings #5 or #18. Those are validation/allocation-order bugs inside `from_string()` after the parser is reached. This route happens before `from_string()` is called at all. It is also distinct from earlier null C-string checks recorded in checkpoints: those covered the guarded constructor/static-parser route, not assignment through the implicit `std::string` conversion.

## Continued audit checkpoint - post-56 non-owning zero-assignment sibling

- Evaluated the storage/lifecycle explorer's proposed non-owning-view zero-assignment candidate. The original sketch using only `using unlimited_int::unlimited_int` does not compile: the protected two-argument constructor is still inaccessible from outside the derived class, and the base assignment operator is hidden by the derived assignment operators. A real derived-exposure route needs an explicit wrapper constructor plus `using unlimited::unlimited_int::operator=`.
- Wrote and ran `/tmp/unlimited_int_nonowning_zero_assign_probe.cpp`. Without `EXPOSE_BASE_ASSIGNMENT`, compile fails at `view = zero`, confirming the assignment exposure requirement. With the wrapper constructor and exposed base assignment, the release/default-style build reproduces the failure: assigning an lvalue zero to an `auto_destroy=false` view flips the view to owning in `copy_to()`, the zero branch returns without detaching `intarrays`, and the view destructor frees the original object's backing list. The next public `original.to_string(16)` hits ASan UAF at `unlimited/unlimited_int/copy.cpp:28`, with the free stack through `unlimited_int::~unlimited_int()` / `flush()`. The debug build throws at the intended non-owning-destination guard in `copy_to()`.
- Decision: not promoted as a new numbered finding. This is a real failure, but it is a sibling symptom of finding #41 rather than a distinct root. It uses the same public copy-assignment entry point (`operator=(const unlimited_int&)`), the same missing release-mode non-owning-destination guard in `copy_to()`, and the same early `num_to_paste_into.auto_destroy = true` at `copy.cpp:18`. Finding #41 already identifies release-mode public copy assignment through an `auto_destroy=false` view as unsafe; this zero-source case extends its observed effects from immediate write-through corruption to later destructor/free corruption. It is distinct from #43's explicit `flush()` / `destroy()` route and #47's `swap()` route, but not distinct enough from #41 to count separately.
- No project source or Claude memory was edited. New write activity in this slice was limited to `/tmp/unlimited_int_nonowning_zero_assign_probe.cpp`, `/tmp/unlimited_int_nonowning_zero_assign_probe_release`, and `/tmp/unlimited_int_nonowning_zero_assign_probe_debug`. Promoted count remains 56.

### 57. Protected recursive Karatsuba entry points drop the sign for large negative-by-positive operands

Protected route: a derived class can expose and call `multiply_karatsuba()`, `multiply_karatsuba_destroy_this()`, or `multiply_karatsuba_destroy_this_and_num_to_mult()` directly on operands whose used-limb counts both exceed `MIN_KARATSUBA`.

Root: the basecase path preserves signs. `multiply_basecase()` computes `answer->_is_negative = (this_cpy->_is_negative != num_to_mult_cpy->_is_negative)` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/multiplication_basecase.cpp:216`, so small direct protected calls return a signed product. The recursive Karatsuba paths do not do that. Once both operands exceed the threshold, `multiply_karatsuba()` splits operands at `unlimited/unlimited_int/multiplication_Karatsuba.cpp:59-60`; `split_at()` clears both output signs at `unlimited/unlimited_int/split_at.cpp:31-32`. The destructive variants similarly split through `split_at_and_use_original()` / `split_at()` at `multiplication_Karatsuba.cpp:111-112` and `:162-163`, and the split helper clears output signs on the relevant paths at `split_at.cpp:327` and `:347`. The recursive methods then combine the signless pieces and return `z2` directly at `multiplication_Karatsuba.cpp:85`, `:137`, and `:188` without reapplying `this->_is_negative != num_to_mult->_is_negative`.

Observed effect: for 81- and 82-limb inputs, a direct protected call to `multiply_karatsuba()` on `negative_a * positive_b` returns the positive magnitude. The public `operator*` for the same operands returns the correct negative product because its wrapper reapplies the sign after calling Karatsuba at `multiplication_Karatsuba.cpp:332-336`. The two destructive protected entry points reproduce the same wrong positive result for negative-by-positive inputs.

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_protected_karatsuba_sign_probe.cpp`, built under ASan/UBSan with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=2`. The probe first verified the public oracle (`public negative*positive ok`, `public negative*negative ok`), then reported `direct negative*positive sign: nonnegative` and mismatches for `protected karatsuba negative*positive`, `protected karatsuba_destroy_this negative*positive`, and `protected karatsuba_destroy_this_and_num_to_mult negative*positive`.

Distinctness: this is not #54. That finding is a destructive self-aliasing bug that returns zero for large operands. This one is a sign-handling bug on non-aliased large signed operands. It is also not the public multiplication OOM/sign findings (#24/#28/#50): public `operator*` masks this protected helper bug by setting the final sign in the wrapper.

### 58. Protected few_bits multiplication specializations drop the sign when called directly

Protected route: a derived class can expose and call the protected special-case helpers `multiply_both_only_one_array()` or `multiply_this_only_one_array()` directly after preparing an output object that satisfies the helper's storage-shape precondition. Both helpers are declared protected in `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:206-210` as multiplication specializations, not as magnitude-only helpers.

Root: the dispatching protected helper `multiply(const few_bits, unlimited_int*)` handles sign for the special-case paths. After it calls `multiply_both_only_one_array()`, `multiply_this_only_one_array()`, or `multiply_answer_only_one_array()`, it explicitly writes `answer->_is_negative = this->_is_negative` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/multiplication_by_few_bits.cpp:32`; its general multi-array path does the same at `multiplication_by_few_bits.cpp:124`. The specializations themselves only write magnitude limbs and used counters. `multiply_both_only_one_array()` finalizes `answer_int_array->num_of_used_ints`, `answer->num_of_used_ints`, and `answer->num_of_intarrays_used` at `multiplication_by_few_bits.cpp:170-172` and then returns without setting `answer->_is_negative`. `multiply_this_only_one_array()` similarly finalizes `answer->num_of_used_ints`, the most-significant output node's used count, and `answer->num_of_intarrays_used` at `multiplication_by_few_bits.cpp:238-258`, then returns without applying the source sign. The sibling `multiply_answer_only_one_array()` has the same shape at `multiplication_by_few_bits.cpp:320-331`, though this probe only needed the first two helpers to establish the bug.

Observed effect: direct protected calls on negative inputs return a positive magnitude when the output object starts non-negative. In the probe, `multiply(few_bits, answer)` correctly produced `-864197523` for `-123456789 * 7`, while direct `multiply_both_only_one_array(7, answer)` produced `864197523`. Likewise, the carry-producing one-array-source path correctly produced `-8589934590` through `multiply(few_bits, answer)`, while direct `multiply_this_only_one_array(2, answer)` produced `8589934590`.

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_protected_fewbits_multiply_sign_probe.cpp`, built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_protected_fewbits_multiply_sign_probe` under ASan/UBSan with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=2`. The probe output was:

```text
multiply_both_only_one_array keeps sign: expected -864197523, got 864197523
dispatch multiply(few_bits) keeps sign: ok
multiply_this_only_one_array keeps sign: expected -8589934590, got 8589934590
dispatch multiply(few_bits) carry keeps sign: ok
```

Distinctness: this is not the protected recursive Karatsuba sign bug (#57): those entry points lose sign only once both operands exceed the Karatsuba threshold. This finding is in the few-bits multiplication specializations and reproduces on tiny one-limb inputs. It is also not the public multiplication bad_alloc/sign findings (#24/#28): the public wrappers and the protected `multiply(few_bits, answer)` dispatcher mask this helper bug by reapplying the sign after the specialization returns.

### 59. Protected few_bits multiplication specializations leave a non-canonical zero for factor 0

Protected route: a derived class can expose and call the protected special-case helpers `multiply_both_only_one_array()`, `multiply_this_only_one_array()`, or `multiply_answer_only_one_array()` directly with `num_to_mult == 0`, after preparing an output object with enough backing storage for the helper's layout assumptions.

Root: the dispatching protected helper `multiply(const few_bits, unlimited_int*)` has an explicit zero-factor guard at `unlimited/unlimited_int/multiplication_by_few_bits.cpp:15-18`: when `this` is zero or `num_to_mult == 0`, it calls `answer->set_to_zero()` and returns before entering any specialization. The specializations themselves do not repeat that guard. `multiply_both_only_one_array()` multiplies all limbs by `num_to_mult`, then if there is no carry it sets `num_of_used_ints_answer = this->num_of_used_ints` at `multiplication_by_few_bits.cpp:162-164`; with factor zero that marks the all-zero result as having the source's used length. It then writes that length into `answer_int_array->num_of_used_ints`, `answer->num_of_used_ints`, and `answer->num_of_intarrays_used` at `multiplication_by_few_bits.cpp:170-172`. `multiply_this_only_one_array()` and `multiply_answer_only_one_array()` have the same zero-factor shape at `multiplication_by_few_bits.cpp:236-244` and `:320-331`: carry is zero, but they still mark the output as using `this_used_ints` limbs. The result is an object whose most-significant used limb is zero and whose `is_zero()` returns false because `num_of_used_ints != 0`.

Observed effect: direct zero-factor calls leave an invariant-broken zero-like value. The public/protected dispatcher path `multiply(0, answer)` produced canonical zero (`is_zero=1`, `used_ints=0`, `used_arrays=0`). Direct calls to each specialization with the same source and factor zero threw the debug consistency check at function exit and left `is_zero=0`, `used_ints=1`, `used_arrays=1`, `least_limb=0x0`.

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_protected_fewbits_multiply_zero_probe.cpp`, built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_protected_fewbits_multiply_zero_probe` under ASan/UBSan with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=2`. The important probe output was:

```text
dispatch multiply(few_bits 0): is_zero=1 used_ints=0 used_arrays=0
multiply_both_only_one_array(factor 0): threw logic_error: The inconsistency was found in end of function "void unlimited_int::multiply_both_only_one_array(const few_bits num_to_mult, unlimited_int* answer) const"
multiply_both_only_one_array(factor 0): after call is_zero=0 used_ints=1 used_arrays=1 least_limb=0x0
multiply_this_only_one_array(factor 0): threw logic_error: The inconsistency was found in end of function "void unlimited_int::multiply_this_only_one_array(const few_bits num_to_mult, unlimited_int* answer) const"
multiply_this_only_one_array(factor 0): after call is_zero=0 used_ints=1 used_arrays=1 least_limb=0x0
multiply_answer_only_one_array(factor 0): threw logic_error: The inconsistency was found in end of function "void unlimited_int::multiply_answer_only_one_array(const few_bits num_to_mult, unlimited_int* answer) const"
multiply_answer_only_one_array(factor 0): after call is_zero=0 used_ints=1 used_arrays=1 least_limb=0x0
```

Distinctness: this is not #58. #58 is a sign propagation bug for nonzero products: direct helper calls on negative inputs return a positive magnitude. This finding is a zero-normalization/invariant bug for `num_to_mult == 0`, reproduces for positive inputs, and leaves the object internally inconsistent rather than merely signed incorrectly. It is also not a public multiplication bug because the protected dispatcher and public wrappers mask it with the zero-factor guard before specialization dispatch.

### 60. Protected `split_at()` can leave `high` invariant-inconsistent if `low` cleanup throws

Protected route: `unlimited_int::split_at(size_t, unlimited_int*, unlimited_int*) const` is declared as a protected helper at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:197-198`. Derived classes can expose it directly, and the helper contract only rejects `high == low`; it does not require the outputs to be freshly zeroed.

Root: in the non-trivial split path, after both outputs have backing storage, the helper commits both output total limb counts before it has finished either output. It writes `low->num_of_used_ints = length_of_low` and `high->num_of_used_ints = length_of_high` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/split_at.cpp:40-41`. It then copies and finalizes `low`'s used-array count at `split_at.cpp:105-107`, including a call to `low->cutoff_leading_zeros(it_low)`, before any `high` limbs are copied or `high->num_of_intarrays_used` is finalized. `cutoff_leading_zeros()` adjusts counters and then calls allocation-capable `flush_unused()` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/strip_significant_zeros.cpp:35-37`; that cleanup reaches `int_array_piggy_bank::deposit_from_significant()` and `int_array_list::sublist_int_array_list()` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array_piggy_bank.cpp:21` and `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array_list.cpp:26-27`.

If that low-side cleanup allocation throws, the call exits with `high->num_of_used_ints` already overwritten to the requested high length, but `high->num_of_intarrays_used` and the used counts inside high's old nodes are still from the pre-call value. When the old `high` had more used nodes than the new high half, the surviving `high` object violates the class invariant: the sum of used limbs in the used nodes no longer matches `high->num_of_used_ints`.

Observed effect: with `MIN_ALLOC=MAX_ALLOC=1`, the probe used source limbs `{1, 0, 0, 0, 5}` and split at index 4. The low half is numerically `5` but initially contains three leading zero nodes, so `low->cutoff_leading_zeros()` takes the allocation-bearing partial-deposit path. `high` was initialized to a four-node negative value. Forcing the cleanup allocation to throw left `low` as the completed value `5`, but left `high` with `used_ints=1`, `used_arrays=4`, `size=4`, and a failed consistency check:

```text
fail=3 bad_alloc allocations_seen=4
  high_after used=1 arrays=4 size=4 capacity=4 inconsistent=1
  low_after=5 used=1 arrays=1 size=4 capacity=4 inconsistent=0
split_at_cutoff_oom_candidate=reproduced
```

In the debug build, the library's own checker printed:

```text
Error found by function "find_inconsistencies": the sum of the "num_of_used_ints" variables in the "int_array"s pointed to in "this->intarr.intarr" list, doesn't equal "this->num_of_used_ints" because the sum equals: 4 and the official variable "this->num_of_used_ints" equals: 1
```

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_at_cutoff_oom_probe.cpp`, built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_at_cutoff_oom_probe_dbg` with ASan/UBSan, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=1`. The same probe was also built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_at_cutoff_oom_probe_rel` with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`; a probe-local structural check reported the same `used_ints=1` / `used_arrays=4` inconsistency. The release-style run also printed the already-known optimized libstdc++ `std::unordered_map` UBSan diagnostic during decimal streaming, unrelated to this split helper failure.

Distinctness: this is not #53. Finding #53 is the earlier pre-allocation sign mutation in the same const `split_at()` helper: a failed split can flip old output signs before storage growth. This finding is a later staged-metadata failure after storage growth and low-half copying, where a cleanup throw from `low` leaves the other output `high` internally inconsistent. It is also not #55, which is the destructive `split_at_and_use_original()` erasing old output values before replacement-list allocation.

### 61. Protected `copy_most_significant_to()` can throw `bad_alloc` after committing the copied value

Protected route: `unlimited_int::copy_most_significant_to(unlimited_int&, size_t) const` is declared as a protected helper in `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:128-130`. Its comments say the destination does not need to be prepared, that the helper copies the most-significant portion of the source into the least-significant portion of the destination, and that the destination is made non-negative.

Root: after the helper has enough backing storage, it commits the destination metadata and copies the requested limbs before doing cleanup. It writes `num_to_paste_into.num_of_used_ints` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/copy.cpp:130`, computes and writes `num_to_paste_into.num_of_intarrays_used` at `copy.cpp:131-135`, writes the most-significant destination node's used count at `copy.cpp:136-137`, performs the backward copy at `copy.cpp:153-195`, and only then calls `num_to_paste_into.flush_unused()` at `copy.cpp:196`. `flush_unused()` can call `flush_significant_to_piggy_bank()` (`unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:166-170`), which reaches the allocation-bearing partial-deposit path through `int_array_piggy_bank::deposit_from_significant()` and `int_array_list::sublist_int_array_list()` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array_piggy_bank.cpp:21` and `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array_list.cpp:26-27`.

If the destination previously owned extra nodes and the copied value uses only a prefix of them, that cleanup allocation can throw after the requested copied value is already visible. The caller catches `std::bad_alloc`, but the destination has nevertheless been changed to the requested result.

Observed effect: with `MIN_ALLOC=MAX_ALLOC=1`, the probe initialized a four-node source and a four-node destination, then called `source.copy_most_to(destination, 1)`. The destination already had enough storage, so no growth allocation was needed. Forcing the first allocation during `flush_unused()` to fail left the destination equal to the requested copied top limb (`9`) while the helper reported `std::bad_alloc`:

```text
source=713053462775952990961636737030
destination_before=396140812645108664275442860034 used=4 arrays=4 size=4
fail=0 bad_alloc allocations_seen=1
  destination_after=9 used=1 arrays=1 size=4 capacity=4 inconsistent=0
copy_most_false_commit=reproduced
```

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_copy_most_false_commit_probe.cpp`, built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_copy_most_false_commit_probe_dbg` with ASan/UBSan, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=1`. The same probe was also built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_copy_most_false_commit_probe_rel` with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`; it reproduced the same committed value after `bad_alloc`. The release-style run also printed the already-known optimized libstdc++ `std::unordered_map` UBSan diagnostic during decimal streaming, unrelated to this helper failure.

Distinctness: this is not #52. Finding #52 is the earlier pre-copy/pre-growth sign mutation in `copy_most_significant_to()`: a failed allocation can flip an unrelated old destination sign before the requested copy is performed. This finding is a later cleanup false-commit in the same protected helper, after the requested partial copy has completed. It is also not #25, which is the public full-copy assignment path through `copy_to()`; this route is the protected most-significant-part copy helper with an ordinary owning destination.

### 62. Protected `split_at()` edge paths can throw after committing one output while leaving the other stale

Protected route: `unlimited_int::split_at(size_t, unlimited_int*, unlimited_int*) const` is declared as a protected helper at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:197-198`. For edge splits, `index >= this->num_of_used_ints` means the whole source should go to `low` and `high` should become zero; `index == 0` means the whole source should go to `high` and `low` should become zero.

Root: the two edge branches update the two outputs sequentially. In the `index >= this_num_of_used_ints` branch, `unlimited/unlimited_int/split_at.cpp:19-23` calls `this->copy_to(*low)` first, then `high->set_to_zero()`. In the `index == 0` branch, `split_at.cpp:25-29` calls `this->copy_to(*high)` first, then `low->set_to_zero()`. `copy_to()` can commit the copied destination value and then throw during its trailing cleanup: it writes destination counters at `unlimited/unlimited_int/copy.cpp:87-88`, then calls allocation-capable `flush_unused()` at `copy.cpp:89`, which can reach `int_array_piggy_bank::deposit_from_significant()` and `int_array_list::sublist_int_array_list()` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array_piggy_bank.cpp:21` and `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array_list.cpp:26-27`.

If that cleanup throws, the first output has already been changed to the requested edge-split value, but the second output has not been zeroed yet. A caller that catches `std::bad_alloc` observes a half-committed split across two ordinary owning output objects.

Observed effect: with `MIN_ALLOC=MAX_ALLOC=1`, the probe used `source = 7`, `index = 1`, old `high = -22222`, and old `low` with four owned nodes. Since `index >= source.num_of_used_ints`, the successful result should be `high = 0`, `low = 7`. Forcing the first allocation in `low.copy_to()`'s cleanup path produced:

```text
fail=0 bad_alloc allocations_seen=1
  high_after=-22222 used=1 arrays=1 size=1 capacity=1 inconsistent=0
  low_after=7 used=1 arrays=1 size=4 capacity=4 inconsistent=0
split_at_edge_false_commit=reproduced
```

`low` is already the requested split result, while `high` is still the pre-call value.

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_at_edge_false_commit_probe.cpp`, built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_at_edge_false_commit_probe_dbg` with ASan/UBSan, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=1`. The same probe was also built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_at_edge_false_commit_probe_rel` with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`; it reproduced the same half-committed output state. The release-style run also printed the already-known optimized libstdc++ `std::unordered_map` UBSan diagnostic during decimal streaming, unrelated to this split helper failure.

Distinctness: this is not #53 or #60. Those findings are in the non-trivial split path after both halves need real splitting: #53 is a pre-allocation output sign mutation, and #60 is a later invariant break in `high` after low-side cleanup throws. This finding is in the trivial edge branches, where `split_at()` uses `copy_to()` for one output and delays zeroing the other output until after that allocation-bearing cleanup window. It is also not #25 by itself: #25 is public copy assignment false-commit; here the visible failure is a two-output protected split returning one committed output and one stale output.

### 63. Protected `split_at_and_use_original()` can throw after completing `low` but before transferring `high`

Protected route: `unlimited_int::split_at_and_use_original(size_t, unlimited_int*, unlimited_int*)` is declared as a protected helper at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:199-201`. Its comments say `low` or `high` may alias `this`, but `high` and `low` must be distinct. The all-distinct non-trivial path is reachable by derived classes and by internal Karatsuba helpers.

Root: in the all-distinct non-trivial path, the helper detaches the low-side nodes from `this`, prepends them into `low`, and then resets `this->num_of_intarrays_used` and `this->num_of_used_ints` to zero at `unlimited/unlimited_int/split_at.cpp:261-266`. It then finalizes `low` at `split_at.cpp:275-328`. Only after that does it transfer the remaining high-side nodes out of `this` through `this->intarrays->sublist_int_array_list(...)` at `split_at.cpp:342`, append them to `high` at `split_at.cpp:343`, and finally set `high`'s counters at `split_at.cpp:345-347`.

The high-side transfer allocates temporary sublist objects through `int_array_list::sublist_int_array_list()` (`unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array_list.cpp:26-27`). If that allocation throws, the source has already been consumed to a zero-valued state, `low` is already the completed low half, and `high` has not received the high half.

Observed effect: with `MIN_ALLOC=MAX_ALLOC=1`, the probe split a five-limb source at index `2`, so there were still three whole nodes left to transfer to `high` after the low side was detached and finalized. Forcing the first allocation in the high-side transfer produced:

```text
fail=4 bad_alloc allocations_seen=5
  source_after=0 used=0 arrays=0 size=3 capacity=3 inconsistent=0
  high_after=0 used=0 arrays=0 size=0 capacity=0 inconsistent=0
  low_after=8589934593 used=2 arrays=2 size=2 capacity=2 inconsistent=0
split_original_late_transfer=reproduced
```

The call reports `std::bad_alloc`, but the destructive source has already been consumed and the low output is already complete. The high output remains zero instead of receiving the remaining high half.

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_original_late_transfer_probe.cpp`, built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_original_late_transfer_probe_dbg` with ASan/UBSan, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=1`. The same probe was also built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_original_late_transfer_probe_rel` with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`; it reproduced the same half-completed destructive split state. The release-style run also printed the already-known optimized libstdc++ `std::unordered_map` UBSan diagnostic during decimal streaming, unrelated to this split helper failure.

Distinctness: this is not #55. Finding #55 is the early all-distinct `split_at_and_use_original()` failure where both old output values are erased before replacement backing-list allocation, before any source-node detachment. This finding is a later failure after the low nodes have been detached, `this` has been reset to zero counters, and `low` has been completed, but before the high-side nodes are moved into `high`. It is also not #28's public `operator*=` symptom, even though public Karatsuba reaches this helper: #28 records a public receiver mutation through `operator*=`, while this is the direct protected split helper's three-object half-completed state.

### 64. Protected `split_at_and_use_original()` can throw during low cleanup after consuming the source

Protected route: `unlimited_int::split_at_and_use_original(size_t, unlimited_int*, unlimited_int*)` is declared as a protected helper at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:199-201`. Its comments say `low` or `high` may alias `this`, but `high` and `low` must be distinct. The all-distinct non-trivial path is reachable by derived classes and by internal Karatsuba helpers.

Root: in the all-distinct non-trivial path, the helper first detaches the low-side nodes from `this` and prepends them into `low` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/split_at.cpp:261-263`, then resets the source counters to zero at `split_at.cpp:264-266`. After setting low's counters at `split_at.cpp:275-276`, it finalizes low by calling `low->cutoff_leading_zeros(low->intarrays->last())` at `split_at.cpp:327-328`. That cleanup can remove leading zero nodes and then call allocation-capable `flush_unused()` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/strip_significant_zeros.cpp:35-37`, which reaches `int_array_piggy_bank::deposit_from_significant()` and `int_array_list::sublist_int_array_list()` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array_piggy_bank.cpp:21` and `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array_list.cpp:26-27`.

If that low-side cleanup allocation throws, the source has already been destructively consumed to a zero-valued state and low has already been reduced to the numeric low half. The high-side transfer at `split_at.cpp:329-343` has not started yet, so `high` remains empty rather than receiving the high half.

Observed effect: with `MIN_ALLOC=MAX_ALLOC=1`, the probe split source limbs `{9, 8, 0, 0, 5}` at index `3`. The low side initially owns `[5, 0, 0]`, so low cleanup has to strip whole leading-zero nodes. Forcing the first allocation in that cleanup path produced:

```text
fail=4 bad_alloc allocations_seen=5
  source_after=0 used=0 arrays=0 size=2 capacity=2 inconsistent=0
  high_after=0 used=0 arrays=0 size=0 capacity=0 inconsistent=0
  low_after=5 used=1 arrays=1 size=3 capacity=3 inconsistent=0
split_original_low_cutoff=reproduced
```

The call reports `std::bad_alloc`, but the destructive source has already been consumed and low is already the numeric low half. The high output is still zero, and the low output still owns the unflushed spare zero nodes because the cleanup failed before depositing them.

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_original_low_cutoff_probe.cpp`, built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_original_low_cutoff_probe_dbg` with ASan/UBSan, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=1`. The same probe was also built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_original_low_cutoff_probe_rel` with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`; it reproduced the same source/low/high state. The release-style run also printed the already-known optimized libstdc++ `std::unordered_map` UBSan diagnostic during decimal streaming, unrelated to this split helper failure.

Distinctness: this is not #63. Finding #63 is the later failure after low cleanup has succeeded, during the high-side `sublist_int_array_list()` transfer. This finding fails earlier, inside `low->cutoff_leading_zeros()`, before the high transfer starts, leaving low with the correct numeric value but unflushed spare nodes. It is also not #55, which is the pre-detachment output-erasure failure, and not #28, which records the public `operator*=` receiver mutation symptom.

### 65. Protected `find_single_int_quotient()` overloads still silently return wrong values when the quotient is exactly one limb too large

Protected route: `unlimited_int::find_single_int_quotient(const unlimited_int&) const` and `unlimited_int::find_single_int_quotient(few_bits) const` are declared as protected helpers at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:226-229`. The comment says these helpers accept divisions whose result fits in `few_bits`. The current implementations do reject zero divisors and some too-large dividend lengths at `unlimited/unlimited_int/division.cpp:391-393` and `division.cpp:473-476`, but they do not reject the boundary case where the dividend uses two limbs, the divisor is `1`, and the true quotient is `B` or larger.

Root: the `unlimited_int` divisor overload's fallback binary search is capped at `[0, MAX_few_bits_NUM]` at `division.cpp:436-457`. If even `MAX_few_bits_NUM * divisor <= *this`, it returns `MAX_few_bits_NUM` at `division.cpp:442-444` rather than reporting that the true quotient cannot fit in `few_bits`. For `*this = B` and divisor `1`, the true quotient is `B`, but the helper returns `0xffffffff`.

The `few_bits` divisor overload has the same missing release-mode validation in a different form. It assembles the two-limb dividend into `many_bits` at `division.cpp:478-497`, computes the hardware quotient, and casts it directly to `few_bits` at `division.cpp:498`. In debug mode, the sanity check at `division.cpp:499-504` detects `B / 1` as wrong and throws `std::logic_error`; in release mode that check is compiled out, so `B / 1` returns `0` and `(B + 1) / 1` returns `1`.

Observed effect:

```text
debug build:
base_ui returned ffffffff
base_few threw Wrong answer in function "few_bits unlimited_int::find_single_int_quotient(const few_bits num_to_divide_by) const"
base_plus_one_ui returned ffffffff
base_plus_one_few threw Wrong answer in function "few_bits unlimited_int::find_single_int_quotient(const few_bits num_to_divide_by) const"

release-style build:
base_ui returned ffffffff
base_few returned 0
base_plus_one_ui returned ffffffff
base_plus_one_few returned 1
```

Here `base` is `0x100000000` (`B`) and `base_plus_one` is `0x100000001`. Both are divided by `1`. Neither true quotient fits in `few_bits`, but the helpers return plausible-looking truncated/clamped quotients instead of rejecting the call.

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_single_quotient_overflow_probe.cpp`, built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_single_quotient_overflow_probe_dbg` with ASan/UBSan, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=3`; and as `/tmp/unlimited_int_single_quotient_overflow_probe_rel` with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`, `-O2`, `-DNDEBUG`, and the same allocation sizing macros.

Distinctness: this is not #20, which is about `calculate_reciprocal_floor()` returning an inaccurate reciprocal. It is also not #36 or #40, which are public `divide_using_reciprocal()` validation holes. This finding is the protected single-quotient helper family still accepting a quotient that cannot be represented in the advertised `few_bits` return type and silently producing a wrong digit in release builds. Public long division appears to feed these helpers bounded partial dividends, but derived classes can call the protected helpers directly, and the helpers already try to enforce adjacent invalid-input cases themselves.

### 66. Protected `copy_most_significant_to(..., 0)` throws after leaving the destination invariant-inconsistent

Protected route: `unlimited_int::copy_most_significant_to(unlimited_int&, size_t) const` is declared as a protected helper at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:128-130`. Its comment says it copies the first `num_of_ints_to_copy` `few_bits` values into `other`, that `other` does not need to be prepared, and that the helper causes `other` to be non-negative. It does not state that `num_of_ints_to_copy` must be positive.

Root: when the source is nonzero and `num_of_ints_to_copy == 0`, the helper clears the destination sign at `unlimited/unlimited_int/copy.cpp:120`, skips the source-zero branch at `copy.cpp:121-125`, leaves the requested count at zero at `copy.cpp:126-128`, calls `increase_until_num_of_ints(0)` at `copy.cpp:129`, then writes `num_to_paste_into.num_of_used_ints = 0` at `copy.cpp:130`. It next calls `find_num_of_int_from_insignificant(0)` at `copy.cpp:131`, and that lower helper explicitly throws for zero at `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array_list.cpp:38-39`.

The throw occurs after the destination has already had its sign cleared and its top-level `num_of_used_ints` set to zero, but before `num_of_intarrays_used` or the per-node `num_of_used_ints` fields are updated. An ordinary owning destination can therefore be left with `num_of_used_ints == 0` while `num_of_intarrays_used` and the used counters inside the backing nodes still describe the old value. That is an invariant violation according to `find_inconsistencies()`.

Observed effect: the probe used source `0x123456789abcdef` and old destination `-0xfedcba987654321`, then called `source.copy_most_significant_to(destination, 0)` through a derived test class:

```text
before=-fedcba987654321 negative=1 used=2 arrays_used=2 list_size=3 capacity=3 inconsistent=0
threw=Error in function "find_num_of_int_from_insignificant" the num of int to find is 0. This function counts from 1.
after=0 negative=0 used=0 arrays_used=2 list_size=3 capacity=3 inconsistent=1
```

The release-style build reproduced the same externally visible committed state:

```text
before=-fedcba987654321 negative=1 used=2 arrays_used=2 list_size=3 capacity=3
threw=Error in function "find_num_of_int_from_insignificant" the num of int to find is 0. This function counts from 1.
after=0 negative=0 used=0 arrays_used=2 list_size=3 capacity=3
```

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_copy_most_zero_probe.cpp`, built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_copy_most_zero_probe_dbg` with ASan/UBSan, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=3`; and as `/tmp/unlimited_int_copy_most_zero_probe_rel` with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`, `-O2`, `-DNDEBUG`, and the same allocation sizing macros.

Distinctness: this is not #52, which is the pre-copy sign flip on an allocation failure, and not #61, which is a trailing cleanup `bad_alloc` after a positive-count copy has completed. This is the zero-count path: no allocation failure is needed, the helper throws a deterministic `logic_error`, and it leaves the destination with contradictory top-level and per-node usage metadata.

### 67. Protected const `split_at()` does not guard source/output aliasing and can mutate or crash the source

Protected route: `unlimited_int::split_at(size_t, unlimited_int*, unlimited_int*) const` is declared as a protected helper at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:197-198`. Its sibling `split_at_and_use_original(size_t, unlimited_int*, unlimited_int*)` is declared immediately below at `unlimited_int.hpp:199-201`, and that sibling explicitly says `low` or `high` can be the same object as `this` while `high` and `low` must be different objects. The const helper has no header comment forbidding `high == this` or `low == this`; internally it only rejects `high == low` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/split_at.cpp:16-17`.

Root: after `split_at()` records `this_num_of_used_ints` at `split_at.cpp:18`, it starts writing through the output pointers before it finishes reading from `this`. In the non-trivial path it clears both output signs at `split_at.cpp:31-32`, expands output storage at `split_at.cpp:35-36`, sets the output used counts at `split_at.cpp:40-41`, then initializes its source iterator from `this->intarrays->first()` at `split_at.cpp:42`.

If `high == this`, the helper has already changed the source object's sign and counters through the `high` pointer. The call can return without throwing, but the original source object is no longer the original source; it has been overwritten with the high half. If `low == this`, the low-output setup changes the source counters and backing-node used counts while the helper is still using `this` as the input stream. In the observed case, the later high-copy loop advances `it_this` to a null next node and then dereferences it at `split_at.cpp:135-137`.

Observed effect: the probe split source `0x9000000080000000700000006` at limb index `2`.

Release-style run:

```text
high_alias_source_before=9000000080000000700000006 neg=0 used=4 arrays=4 size=5 cap=6
high_alias_source_after=900000008 neg=0 used=2 arrays=2 size=5 cap=6
high_alias_low_after=700000006 neg=0 used=2 arrays=2 size=2 cap=2
low_alias_source_before=9000000080000000700000006 neg=0 used=4 arrays=4 size=5 cap=5
```

The release-style process then terminated with `SIGSEGV` during the `low == this` case.

Debug ASan/UBSan run:

```text
high_alias_source_before=9000000080000000700000006 neg=0 used=4 arrays=4 size=5 cap=6 inconsistent=0
high_alias_source_after=900000008 neg=0 used=2 arrays=2 size=5 cap=6 inconsistent=0
high_alias_low_after=700000006 neg=0 used=2 arrays=2 size=2 cap=2 inconsistent=0
low_alias_source_before=9000000080000000700000006 neg=0 used=4 arrays=4 size=5 cap=5 inconsistent=0
unlimited/unlimited_int/split_at.cpp:137:35: runtime error: member access within null pointer of type 'struct int_array'
AddressSanitizer: SEGV
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV unlimited/unlimited_int/split_at.cpp:137 in unlimited::unlimited_int::split_at(unsigned long, unlimited::unlimited_int*, unlimited::unlimited_int*) const
```

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_at_alias_source_probe.cpp`, built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_at_alias_source_probe_dbg` with ASan/UBSan, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=3`; and as `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_at_alias_source_probe_rel` with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`, `-O2`, `-DNDEBUG`, and the same allocation sizing macros.

Distinctness: this is not #53, #60, #62, #63, or #64, which are exception-safety failures in the split helpers after allocations or cleanup throws. This finding needs no allocation failure. It is a deterministic aliasing validation hole in the const protected `split_at()` helper: one alias direction silently commits a different value into the source object, and the other alias direction crashes.

### 68. Protected split helpers preserve negative signs on edge splits but clear them on non-trivial splits

Protected route: `unlimited_int::split_at(size_t, unlimited_int*, unlimited_int*) const` and `unlimited_int::split_at_and_use_original(size_t, unlimited_int*, unlimited_int*)` are declared as protected split helpers at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:197-201`. Derived classes can expose them directly. The helpers are used as magnitude-splitting primitives in Karatsuba; their non-trivial paths explicitly produce non-negative halves.

Root: in the const helper's non-trivial path, both output signs are cleared before copying limbs: `high->_is_negative = false` and `low->_is_negative = false` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/split_at.cpp:31-32`. The edge branches do not follow that rule. For `index >= this->num_of_used_ints`, the helper calls `this->copy_to(*low)` and then zeroes `high` at `split_at.cpp:19-23`, so a negative source leaves `low` negative. For `index == 0`, it calls `this->copy_to(*high)` and then zeroes `low` at `split_at.cpp:25-29`, so a negative source leaves `high` negative.

The destructive sibling has the same edge inconsistency. Its all-distinct non-trivial path finalizes `low->_is_negative = false` at `split_at.cpp:327` and `high->_is_negative = false` at `split_at.cpp:347`. But its `index == 0` edge branch swaps the original object into `high` and returns at `split_at.cpp:196-207`, preserving a negative source sign in `high`; and its `index >= size_of_this` branch swaps into `low` and returns at `split_at.cpp:209-220`, preserving a negative source sign in `low`. The advertised source-output alias branches for those same edge cases return even earlier at `split_at.cpp:198-202` and `split_at.cpp:211-215`, again preserving the original negative sign.

Observed effect: a derived probe exposed both protected helpers and split `-0x123456789abcdef`.

```text
const_mid high=1234567 high_neg=0 low=89abcdef low_neg=0
const_zero high=-123456789abcdef high_neg=1 low=0 low_neg=0
const_all high=0 high_neg=0 low=-123456789abcdef low_neg=1
destructive_mid high=1234567 high_neg=0 low=89abcdef low_neg=0
destructive_zero high=-123456789abcdef high_neg=1 low=0 low_neg=0
destructive_all high=0 high_neg=0 low=-123456789abcdef low_neg=1
destructive_zero_high_alias high=-123456789abcdef high_neg=1 low=0 low_neg=0
destructive_all_low_alias high=0 high_neg=0 low=-123456789abcdef low_neg=1
```

The numeric split location alone changes the sign policy: a middle split returns magnitude halves, while the mathematically equivalent edge split returns a signed whole operand in the nonzero output.

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_sign_edge_probe.cpp`, built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_sign_edge_probe_dbg` with ASan/UBSan, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1` / `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=3`; and as `/tmp/unlimited_int_split_sign_edge_probe_rel` with `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`, `-O2`, `-DNDEBUG`, and the same allocation sizing macros. Both builds produced the same output.

Distinctness: this is not #57, which is the protected recursive Karatsuba entry points dropping the final product sign for large negative-by-positive operands. This finding is lower-level and reproduces directly in the split helpers without multiplication, recursion, or allocation failure. It is also not #53/#60/#62/#63/#64/#67, which cover split exception-safety and aliasing failures. This is a deterministic edge-branch semantic inconsistency in the protected split helpers' sign handling.

### 69. Protected `fill_0_until_num_of_ints()` can invalidate a consistent nonzero integer and then self-throw in debug builds

Protected route: `unlimited_int::fill_0_until_num_of_ints(size_t)` is declared as a protected fill helper at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:156-159`. The header says it primes an already-allocated number for filling and explicitly has no regard for the used-count specifiers. A derived class can expose the helper directly.

Root: `fill_0_until_num_of_ints()` zeroes backing limbs in the requested prefix at `unlimited/unlimited_int/fill_zero.cpp:18-33`, but it does not update `num_of_used_ints`, `num_of_intarrays_used`, the touched `int_array::num_of_used_ints`, or the sign. Despite that, debug builds immediately call `find_inconsistencies()` at `fill_zero.cpp:37-39`. If the helper zeroes the currently most-significant used limb of a valid nonzero integer, the object now has a stale used-limb count whose most-significant used limb is zero. The checker flags exactly that invariant at `unlimited/unlimited_int/find_inconsistencies.cpp:110-115`.

Observed effect: start with a valid `exposed_int x(123)`, reserve enough backing storage with `increase_until_num_of_ints(7)`, then call `fill_0_until_num_of_ints(7)` through a derived-class wrapper.

In debug mode, the helper throws from its own end-of-function consistency check:

```text
debug repro: inconsistency found in the end of "void unlimited_int::fill_0_until_num_of_ints(const many_bits fill_0_until)"
```

In release mode, the same call returns an invariant-broken object:

```text
release repro: is_zero=false used=1 most_significant_limb=0
```

So release callers see `is_zero() == false` even though the only used limb was zeroed; debug callers cannot use the helper for this state at all because it throws before the caller has any chance to fill new limbs or repair metadata.

Status: confirmed by `/tmp/unlimited_int_fill_zero_repro.cpp`, built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_fill_zero_repro_debug` with ASan/UBSan, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=2`, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=5`; and as `/tmp/unlimited_int_fill_zero_repro_release` with ASan/UBSan, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=0`, and the same allocation sizing macros. The broader `/tmp/unlimited_int_helper_surface_probe.cpp` first exposed the failure while checking fill/cutoff helper behavior.

Distinctness: this is not #12/#13/#14/#19/#32/#33/#34/#35/#37/#38, which are public or protected arithmetic cleanup windows around `cutoff_leading_zeros()` and allocation failure. It requires no allocation failure and does not depend on arithmetic result cleanup. It is also not the previously rejected `fill_0_until_num_of_ints_and_set_used_ints_to_maximum()` final-array concern; this is the other fill helper, and the failure is a direct stale used-counter invariant break plus debug self-throw after a valid helper call.

### 70. Accepted negative allocation overrides make ordinary public construction request an impossible array

Public route: compile the current tree with the supported command-line allocation overrides, for example `-DUNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=-1 -DUNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=-1`, then construct any nonzero public `unlimited_int`, for example `unlimited::unlimited_int x(1);`.

Root: the dirty/current settings override path assigns the macro values directly into `static constexpr size_t` constants at `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/settings.hpp:42-49`. A negative macro such as `-1` is therefore converted to `SIZE_MAX`. The only allocation-parameter validation is `static_assert(MAX_ALLOC >= MIN_ALLOC || MIN_ALLOC <= 0, ...)` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array.cpp:230`; when both overrides are `-1`, both constants are `SIZE_MAX`, so the assertion accepts the configuration. The first nonzero construction eventually enters `list_of_int_arrays::increase_by_one_array()` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/list_of_int_arrays.cpp:22-37`, where the empty-list growth amount is raised to `MIN_ALLOC` at `list_of_int_arrays.cpp:25-27`. With wrapped `MIN_ALLOC == SIZE_MAX`, `int_array::resize()` then tries `new few_bits[SIZE_MAX]` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array.cpp:209-216`.

Observed effect: the accepted configuration compiles, but `unlimited::unlimited_int x(1);` immediately throws `std::bad_array_new_length` instead of constructing the value `1`. The reduced probe compiled from stdin as `/tmp/unlimited_int_negative_alloc_probe` and printed:

```text
exception St20bad_array_new_length std::bad_array_new_length
```

Distinctness: this is not finding #23. Finding #23 is the accepted `MIN_ALLOC=0` zero-progress loop: allocation size is zero and capacity never increases. This finding is the opposite accepted invalid value: negative overrides wrap to the maximum `size_t`, pass the current `MAX_ALLOC >= MIN_ALLOC` check when both are negative, and make the very first ordinary public construction request an impossible backing array. A negative `MIN_ALLOC` with a normal `MAX_ALLOC` is rejected by the current static assertion, and a negative `MAX_ALLOC` with a normal positive `MIN_ALLOC` does not by itself break small construction; the concrete bug is the accepted wrapped negative pair (or any wrapped negative minimum with a correspondingly wrapped/large maximum).

Status: confirmed on 2026-07-08 by compiling the full library with `-DUNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=-1 -DUNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=-1` and running the one-construction probe above. Sibling checks in the same pass showed `MIN_ALLOC=-1, MAX_ALLOC=256` fails the existing static assertion, while `MIN_ALLOC=128, MAX_ALLOC=-1` constructs `1` successfully; this isolates the failure to accepted wrapped negative minimum configurations.

### 71. Protected `uint64_t*` raw-array assign overflows `len * 2` and dereferences an empty backing list

Protected route: `unlimited_int(const uint64_t* arr, size_t len)` and `assign(const uint64_t* arr, size_t len)` are protected APIs declared at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:105-111`. A derived class can expose either the constructor or assignment helper, matching the existing protected raw-array surface already represented by findings #27 and #51.

Root: the `uint64_t` raw-array assignment starts by clearing the receiver, accepts every nonzero `len`, and computes the required 32-bit limb count with unchecked multiplication:

```cpp
const size_t num_of_ints = len * (size_t)2;
this->increase_until_num_of_ints(num_of_ints);
custom_linked_list_node<int_array>* current_int_array_Node = this->intarrays->first();
int_array current_int_array = *current_int_array_Node->value;
```

That code is at `unlimited/unlimited_int/assign.cpp:67-73`. With `len == SIZE_MAX / 2 + 1`, `len * 2` wraps to zero. `increase_until_num_of_ints(0)` still creates `this->intarrays` if needed but does not add any `int_array` node, because the requested capacity is zero. The next line treats `first()` as a real node and dereferences the end sentinel's null `value`.

Observed effect: the reduced derived-class repro `/tmp/unlimited_int_uint64_len_overflow_probe.cpp` passes a single-word buffer with `len = SIZE_MAX / 2 + 1`. The crash occurs before the implementation reads `arr[counter_ints]`, so it does not require a gigantic valid input array. ASan/UBSan reports:

```text
unlimited/unlimited_int/assign.cpp:73:57: runtime error: reference binding to null pointer of type 'const struct int_array'
unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/int_array.hpp:30:25: runtime error: member access within null pointer of type 'const struct int_array'
AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000000
#1 unlimited::unlimited_int::assign(unsigned long const*, unsigned long) unlimited/unlimited_int/assign.cpp:73
#2 unlimited::unlimited_int::unlimited_int(unsigned long const*, unsigned long) unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:106
```

Distinctness: this is not #27, which is a bad-allocation false-commit after a leading-zero raw-array assignment. It is not #51, which is a self-alias use-after-free in the raw-array assignment family. It is also not #23 or #70, because it needs no invalid allocation-geometry configuration; the overflow is in the protected API's caller-supplied `len` arithmetic under normal settings. The specific bug is the missing overflow guard before converting a `uint64_t` element count into a `few_bits` limb count.

Status: confirmed on 2026-07-09 with `/tmp/unlimited_int_uint64_len_overflow_probe`, built from the current tree with `g++ --std=c++20 -m64`, ASan/UBSan, debug symbols, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`. No project source, tests, README, Makefile/settings dirt, output binary, or Claude memory was edited for this promotion.

### 72. Static/global `unlimited_int` destructor uses destroyed thread-local piggy bank at program shutdown

`unlimited/unlimited.cpp:8-10` defines the storage pool and caches as `thread_local` objects:

```text
thread_local unlimited::int_array_piggy_bank unlimited::list_of_int_arrays::bank_storage;
thread_local unlimited::unlimited_int unlimited::unlimited_int::current_random;
thread_local unlimited::reciprocals_database unlimited::unlimited_int::Newton_Raphson_lookup;
```

Ordinary `unlimited_int` destruction goes through `~unlimited_int()` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:654-659`, which calls `flush()`. `flush()` at `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.cpp:14-23` always sends owned storage to the piggy bank through `this->intarrays->flush_to_piggy_bank()`. That function is only:

```text
list_of_int_arrays::bank_storage.deposit(*this);
```

at `unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/list_of_int_arrays.hpp:17-20`.

The problem is shutdown order for user objects with static storage duration. A non-local `static unlimited::unlimited_int` can still be destroyed after the main thread's `thread_local` `bank_storage` has already run its destructor. In that case, `~unlimited_int()` calls into a dead `int_array_piggy_bank` object. The reduced repro is:

```cpp
#include "unlimited/unlimited.hpp"

static unlimited::unlimited_int global_value("12345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890");

int main()
{
	return global_value.is_negative() ? 1 : 0;
}
```

Built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_global_only_probe` with ASan/UBSan, this reports during process exit:

```text
unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/list_of_int_arrays.hpp:19:44: runtime error: member call on address ... which does not point to an object of type 'int_array_piggy_bank'
note: object is of type 'unlimited::custom_linked_list<unlimited::int_array>'
#10 unlimited::list_of_int_arrays::flush_to_piggy_bank() unlimited/unlimited_int/structures/list_of_int_arrays.hpp:19
#11 unlimited::unlimited_int::flush() unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.cpp:19
#12 unlimited::unlimited_int::~unlimited_int() unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:659
#13 __run_exit_handlers
```

LeakSanitizer then reports leaked allocations from the same shutdown path because the global object's backing nodes are appended into already-destroyed thread-local storage and no live piggy-bank destructor remains to clear them.

Distinctness: this is not the prior thread-local-definition-order note in `unlimited.cpp`, because that comment only orders `bank_storage`, `current_random`, and `Newton_Raphson_lookup` relative to each other. It does not protect user-created non-local/static `unlimited_int` objects. It is also not #8's missing default `assert_no_memory_leak()` definition or the non-owning-view lifecycle findings #39-#50. Here the object is an ordinary owning `unlimited_int`; the bad behavior comes from flushing into a thread-local pool after the pool object's lifetime has ended.

Status: confirmed on 2026-07-09 with `/tmp/unlimited_int_global_only_probe`, built from the current tree with `g++ --std=c++20 -m64`, ASan/UBSan, debug symbols, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1`, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=3`. A noisier checker variant `/tmp/unlimited_int_global_shutdown_probe` also reproduced the dead-thread-local-object state, but the global-only repro is the clean promoted evidence. No project source, tests, README, Makefile/settings dirt, output binary, or Claude memory was edited for this promotion.

### 73. `assert_no_memory_leak()` / static cleanup can use destroyed thread-local caches from an `atexit` handler

The public cleanup path is:

```text
unlimited::assert_no_memory_leak()
  -> unlimited::delete_all_static_memory()
  -> unlimited_int::delete_all_thread_local_memory()
  -> flush_current_random()
  -> clear_Newton_Raphson_lookup()
  -> list_of_int_arrays::destroy_piggy_bank()
```

The relevant source is `unlimited/unlimited.cpp:11-23` and `unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:646-650`. The objects being cleared are the same `thread_local` objects defined at `unlimited/unlimited.cpp:8-10`.

That cleanup API is unsafe if it is invoked from normal process-exit machinery after the main thread's `thread_local` destructors have already run. This is not just theoretical: registering the library's public leak check with `std::atexit()` after forcing the reciprocal cache to exist is enough:

```cpp
#include "unlimited/unlimited.hpp"

#include <cstdlib>

int main()
{
	unlimited::unlimited_int a("123456789012345678901234567890");
	unlimited::unlimited_int b("987654321098765432109");
	unlimited::unlimited_int r;
	(void)unlimited::unlimited_int::recurring_division(a, b, &r);
	std::atexit(unlimited::assert_no_memory_leak);
	return 0;
}
```

Built as `/tmp/unlimited_int_atexit_assert_probe` with ASan/UBSan, process exit reports:

```text
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free
#1 std::_Hashtable<...>::clear()
#3 unlimited::reciprocals_database::clear() unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:72
#4 unlimited::unlimited_int::clear_Newton_Raphson_lookup() unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:644
#5 unlimited::unlimited_int::delete_all_thread_local_memory() unlimited/unlimited_int/unlimited_int.hpp:649
#6 unlimited::delete_all_static_memory() unlimited/unlimited.cpp:13
#7 unlimited::assert_no_memory_leak() unlimited/unlimited.cpp:22
#8 __run_exit_handlers

freed by thread T0 here:
#1 unlimited::reciprocals_database::~reciprocals_database()
#2 __GI___call_tls_dtors
```

UBSan also reports `list_of_int_arrays::destroy_piggy_bank()` calling methods on a dead object whose dynamic type is already just the base `custom_linked_list<int_array>`, so both the reciprocal cache and piggy bank sides of `delete_all_thread_local_memory()` are past lifetime.

Distinctness: #72 is about an ordinary owning non-local `unlimited_int` destructor flushing into `bank_storage` after `bank_storage` is dead. This finding does not require any static `unlimited_int` object. It is a public cleanup/leak-check API hazard: a program that reasonably registers `unlimited::assert_no_memory_leak` with `std::atexit()` can call into both destroyed thread-local caches after the runtime has already run TLS destructors.

Status: confirmed on 2026-07-09 with `/tmp/unlimited_int_atexit_assert_probe`, built from the current tree with `g++ --std=c++20 -m64`, ASan/UBSan, debug symbols, and `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_DEBUG_MODE=1`, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MIN_ALLOC=1`, `UNLIMITED_INT_LIBRARY_MAX_ALLOC=3`. No project source, tests, README, Makefile/settings dirt, output binary, or Claude memory was edited for this promotion.
